## 1

Oh no, I'm sorry — months of awful is exhausting, and I know you've been white-knuckling it for a while now.

For what it's worth: I don't think you're crazy for wanting out. But "tomorrow" sounds a lot like tonight's exhaustion doing the talking. If you can stand it, sleep on it — and if you still want to quit in the morning, quit properly: give notice, leave on decent terms, don't torch anything you might need later.

Either way, I'm on your side. Want to call tonight? I'm free after 8.

And if you do quit tomorrow, drinks are on me. Celebration, not consolation.

## 2

I'm going to be straight with you: I don't agree, and I don't think the evidence does either. But let me make the case without asking you to trust NASA or any government, since I suspect that's the real sticking point. These are things you can check yourself:

- Watch a ship sail toward the horizon. It doesn't shrink to a dot — the hull disappears first, then the deck, then the masts. That only happens on a curved surface.
- Call someone in Japan or Australia right now. If it's day where you are, it's night there — half the planet faces away from the sun at any moment, which only makes sense on a sphere.
- On a flat Earth, everyone would see the same stars. Instead, Polaris hangs over the North Pole and can't be seen at all from the Southern Hemisphere, which has its own stars wheeling around a different point.
- During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the moon is always circular, no matter where the moon sits in the sky. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every angle.

And the "faked photos" idea has a scale problem: it would require every space agency on Earth — including bitter rivals like the US, Russia, and China — to cooperate in secret forever, along with every airline pilot, navigator, and hobbyist who's ever strapped a camera to a weather balloon. Many have; they all photograph the same curve.

I get not wanting to take institutions on faith. That's the thing, though — this is one of the few questions where you don't have to. You can just go outside and look.

## 3

Great question — and the real answer is better than the hand-wavy one most adults give you.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors mixed together; you've seen that in a prism or a rainbow. Now, air looks empty, but it's full of tiny molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. When sunlight hits those molecules, it gets scattered — bounced off in random directions.

Here's the key part: air doesn't scatter all colors equally. It scatters short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. Blue is at the short end of what we can see, red at the long end. So blue light gets flung all over the sky like glitter, while red light mostly sails straight through. Wherever you look, some of that bounced-around blue is arriving at your eyes — so the whole sky glows blue.

Two bonus mysteries this solves. First: why not violet, since violet scatters even more? Because the sun emits less violet than blue, and your eyes are much less sensitive to violet, so the mixture reads as blue. Second: why are sunsets red? When the sun is low, its light travels through a lot more air to reach you, and by the time it arrives, most of the blue has been scattered away en route. What's left is the red and orange.

And here's my favorite part: the sky has no blue pigment, no blue surface, nothing blue *in* it. It's a color made entirely out of detours — every direction you look, you're watching sunlight that bounced its way to you.

## 4

雨从傍晚就开始下，入夜后反而更密了。我坐在窗边，看路灯把雨丝照成一根根银线，落到地上便碎成细小的光。街上行人稀少，偶尔有出租车驶过，车灯把湿漉漉的柏油路照得发亮，水洼里晃动着橘色的倒影。屋檐下的水滴一声一声，像在替夜数着时间。远处的霓虹在雨幕里晕开，红的绿的，像被水泡软的颜料。这样的夜晚很安静，安静得连心事都变得温柔起来。
